meta.title: Towards Automated Grain Size Analysis for ExoMars: Preliminary Results from the GRAINS Project
meta.authorsHtml: Cristina Luna<sup>†</sup><sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Almudena Moreno<sup>†</sup><sup>1</sup>, Augusto Gómez Eguíluz<sup>1</sup>, Guillermo Algarabel<sup>1</sup>, Sergio Álvarez<sup>1</sup>, Joanna Kozakiewicz<sup>2</sup>, Alexander M. abstract: Grain size is a fundamental descriptor of sedimentary material. For the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin Rover, it carries direct relevance to the search for preserved organic matter at Oxia Planum. However, laboratory sieving and manual photosieving are both incompatible with the operational timeline of the mission, making automated image-based granulometry a necessity rather than a convenience. This paper reviews the progression of image-based grain size methods with emphasis on deep learning segmentation, and identifies the ImageGrains 2.0 framework as the most suitable current approach for planetary deployment. We describe its adaptation within the GRAINS project, including the camera and illumination setup used to acquire PanCam and CLUPI representative analogue imagery, and present preliminary segmentation and grain size results obtained on a dataset of 21 Antarctic analogue samples that is now being extended to further Mars analogue materials.

blocks.html: The ExoMars Rosalind Franklin Rover will land at Oxia Planum in 2030, a site selected for its clay-bearing phyllosilicate units interpreted as products of sustained Noachian water-rock interaction [1], and grain size distribution is a direct proxy for the transport energy and depositional environment that controlled the preservation of any organic signal in these units [2]. The rover carries two cameras capable of resolving individual grains, PanCam [3] down to approximately 0.3 mm pixel<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup> at close range and CLUPI [4] below 0.1 mm at minimum working distance. The nominal 218-sol mission and its demanding planning cycle preclude the several hours of manual expert processing typically required for a single Folk and Ward characterisation [5]. Automated grain size analysis of rover imagery is therefore operationally necessary. However, despite substantial prior manual and semi-automated work on MER, Phoenix, and MSL imagery [6–9], no automated granulometry tool has been deployed operationally on a Mars mission to date.

Before the advent of deep learning, image-based granulometry on Earth relied on several main approaches. Photosieving digitises individual grain outlines to reproduce sieve-equivalent size classes [2]. However, it is limited to coarse material and typically requires roughly an hour of analyst time per image. Automated boundary-detection algorithms extend this method to unsupervised operation, although their performance degrades under dust contamination and low contrast [10, 11]. Spatial autocorrelation of image intensity avoids grain delineation entirely, but it requires a calibration library spanning the target grain-size range [12]. By contrast, wavelet decomposition of image texture removes the calibration requirement, though stable statistics generally require on the order of a thousand resolved grains per image [13, 14].

Convolutional regression networks such as SediNet predict Folk and Ward statistics directly from image patches without any intermediate grain detection, which makes them particularly suited to fine or heavily compacted surfaces where boundary delineation fails but the global texture signal remains informative [15]. Instance segmentation architectures take the opposite approach by delineating individual grains. These methods range from the fully convolutional patch aggregation used in GRAINet [16], to Mask R-CNN fine-tuned through transfer learning from biomedical cell segmentation [17], to the prompt-based use of the Segment Anything Model in Segmenteverygrain [18]. Their main advantage is that they provide per-grain measurements. However, their performance degrades when grain boundaries are indistinct, and they typically require greater computational resources.

Among these methods, ImageGrains 2.0 provides the strongest combination of properties for planetary deployment [19]. It re-trains the Cellpose-SAM foundation model on a dataset of more than 29,000 manually annotated grains spanning fluvial gravel, glaciofluvial and bioclastic sediment, and X-ray computed tomography imagery. Across all image types tested, it outperforms SAM, Segmenteverygrain, and the previous Cellpose-based ImageGrains model by up to 20% in AP@0.5 and mean average precision. It also recovers grain-size distributions that are statistically indistinguishable from ground truth in the large majority of cases. In addition, it tolerates grain overlap and nongrain clutter, such as shadows, scale bars, and vegetation, without being trained specifically to reject them. Finally, it can be fine-tuned to a new imaging context with as few as seven additional annotated tiles, rather than requiring a new large training campaign. On this basis, the proposed approach relies on ImageGrains 2.0 as the segmentation backbone for the GRAINS project.

The ImageGrains 2.0 workflow segments images with a Cellpose-SAM model. This model combines the SAM vision transformer encoder with the Cellpose gradient flow decoder and was re-trained on the IG2 dataset for 500 epochs. Ellipses are then fitted to the resulting grain masks to derive per-grain axis lengths, together with the standard shape descriptors of convexity, isoperimetric ratio and eccentricity, i.e. typically used in Folk and Ward grain size statistics.

Once trained, the model requires no per-site calibration. It is also robust to the imbalance between subsets of very different sample size. In addition, its 3D extension has been demonstrated on stacked X-ray computed tomography imagery, which is directly relevant to the layered analogue sample geometry used in GRAINS.

The GRAINS project adapts the ImageGrains 2.0 Cellpose- SAM architecture to the imaging conditions and scientific requirements of the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin Rover, extending the training dataset with terrestrial Mars-analogue imagery acquired with camera and illumination surrogates for PanCam HRC and CLUPI.

Two commercial cameras were selected as physical emulators of the flight instruments, following the same acquisition philosophy as the AUPE-2 PanCam HRC emulator and the Canon EOS M50 CLUPI emulator validated by [20]. Table 1 summarises the principal characteristics of the Pan- Cam HRC and CLUPI cameras, together with those of their respective analogues. PanCam HRC is represented by an AVT Manta G-146C with a Computar M5018-MP2 50 mm lens. Although this camera has a smaller sensor, a coarser pixel pitch and a wider native field of view than PanCam HRC, it can be configured to provide a close approximation in grain-scale sampling and effective field of view by placing the camera at approximately 1.75 m for the 2 m PanCam mast reference height and cropping the output to 1024×1024 pixels. CLUPI is represented by a Sigma SD15 with a 105 mm macro lens, which matches CLUPI in sensor dimensions, pixel pitch, resolution and Foveon-type full-colour architecture, with the main limitation being its 31.5 cm minimum focusing distance. Therefore, the Sigma-based imagery is representative of CLUPI within the overlapping focus range rather than across its full operating envelope.

Illumination is provided by two light sources combined to span three contrast regimes. Diffuse near-frontal lighting reproduces the low-contrast conditions reported as challenging for CLUPI-like imagery [20]. Moderate oblique incidence provides an intermediate level of contrast. Grazing directional illumination maximises relief-driven texture and shadowing. Therefore, the dataset samples both favourable and difficult imaging conditions rather than a single idealised one.

Using this camera and illumination setup, a dataset has been acquired on 21 types of Antarctic analogue soil and sediment samples (see Figure 1), each imaged under the PanCam and CLUPI equivalent configurations and across the low, intermediate and high contrast illumination regimes described above, and this dataset is currently being extended with additional Mars-analogue materials to broaden the range of grain morphology, sorting and mineralogy represented in the training and validation sets.

blocks.title: Baseline performance on historical Mars imagery

blocks.html: The ImageGrains 2.0 model, without any Mars-specific retraining, was applied to a set of over 400 close-up images from past Mars missions, spanning the MER Microscopic Imager and MSL MAHLI archives. From this initial dataset, 62 different types of grains were identified and classified. To obtain a more balanced and diverse dataset, a representative subset of 256 images was selected. From this subset, 25 images were manually annotated to provide ground truth grain masks.

The initial application of ImageGrains 2.0 to the full set of more than 400 images showed that, although the model did not perform consistently across all Martian images, it had already learned image features that were relevant for the GRAINS model. This model therefore provided a suitable starting point for transfer learning. Building on this baseline, the next stage focused on developing the GRAINS model by fine-tuning and retraining ImageGrains 2.0 with the newly curated Mars-analogue dataset.

blocks.html: Comparison against the manually annotated subset reveals systematic degradation relative to the terrestrial IG2 benchmark, concentrated in a small number of recurring conditions rather than distributed uniformly across the dataset. This is particularly relevant for planetary applications, where image-based granulometry is strongly dependent on grain visibility, spatial resolution, and the contrast of grain boundaries. Three main failure modes have been identified:
1. Limited grain resolution. Grains smaller than approximately 10 pixels in characteristic diameter approach the effective resolution limit of the imagery.
At this scale, grain boundaries are represented by only a small number of pixels and can become blurred or
indistinguishable from the surrounding material, reducing the reliability of grain detection and segmentation.

2. Strongly mixed grain size populations. Images containing a broad range of grain sizes tend to bias the segmentation toward larger and more visually prominent particles. Smaller grains, particularly when they are only weakly resolved, can be overlooked or merged with neighbouring grains or background material. Consequently, the recovered grain size distribution may underrepresent the finer fraction of heterogeneous sediments.

3. Mixed grain morphologies. Images containing grains with strongly variable shapes, irregular boundaries, or substantial overlap pose an additional challenge. Models trained predominantly on more regular, well-sorted grains have difficulty identifying individual particle boundaries when morphology varies substantially within the same image. Boundary ambiguity and grain contact can lead to incomplete segmentation, merging of adjacent grains, or incorrect delineation of individual particles.

The principal limitations of the baseline model are associated with specific combinations of image resolution, grain size heterogeneity, and morphological complexity. Therefore, they provide a direct basis for selecting and curating additional training data for the Mars-oriented model.

The GRAINS analogue dataset, currently comprising over 1000 images across 21 Antarctic samples and expanding to further Mars-analogue materials, is being extended and curated specifically to target the failure modes identified above rather than as a generic enlargement of the training set.

The retraining strategy therefore prioritizes the inclusion of examples that reproduce the most challenging conditions observed. In particular, the dataset is being expanded with images that contain poorly resolved small grains, broad and heterogeneous grain size distributions, and a wider diversity of grain morphologies. These additions are intended to expose the model more systematically to cases in which grain boundaries are weak and particle sizes differ substantially within the same field of view.

blocks.html: A first fine-tuning experiment has already been conducted using the subset of manually annotated images currently available. This initial retraining should be regarded as a proof of concept rather than as the final GRAINS model, since the annotation campaign is still ongoing and the training dataset does not yet represent the full range of grain sizes, morphologies and imaging conditions targeted by the project. Nevertheless, the preliminary results indicate that the pre-trained model can be effectively adapted to the Martian image domain. As illustrated in Figure 2, fine-tuning can substantially improve grain delineation in cases where the original ImageGrains 2.0 model produces incomplete segmentation.

A preliminary quantitative evaluation was performed on a held-out test subset comprising seven manually annotated images. The retrained GRAINS model improved all evaluated segmentation and granulometric metrics relative to ImageGrains 2.0 (see results in Table 2). Mean AP50 increased from 0.599 to 0.714 and the mean F1 score from 0.715 to 0.818. Improvements were also observed in the derived granulometry, with the median grain-diameter error decreasing from 7.9% to 0.7%, the median grain-count error decreasing from −26.8% to −4.4%, and the median Wasserstein distance decreasing from 2.10 pixels to 1.03 pixels.

This paper adapts an automated granulometry model to the imaging conditions of the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin Rover. The GRAINS approach builds on ImageGrains 2.0, combining Mars-analogue image acquisition, targeted dataset curation and transfer learning to close the gap observed when the terrestrial model is applied to historical Martian imagery.

Grain-count and diameter errors are median relative errors, the Wasserstein distance quantifies the difference between predicted and manually annotated grain-size distributions.

blocks.html: The preliminary results indicate that domain-specific fine-tuning can improve both grain segmentation and the granulometric information derived from the predicted masks. On the current seven-image held-out subset, the retrained model outperforms ImageGrains 2.0 on every evaluated metric and reduces grain-count and diameter errors substantially.

These results are preliminary. The annotation campaign is ongoing, the training dataset does not yet cover the full range of grain sizes, morphologies and imaging conditions targeted by GRAINS, and the test subset remains small. Next steps are expanding the annotated dataset, repeating the fine-tuning and validating the final model on a larger, independent set.
